title: Your simran
hookLine: settle on a time and a length that fits your life
last: SIMRAN — HANDS AT WORK, HEART AT HOME.

lines: A PLAN THAT FITS YOUR LIFE.
cards: Every January, someone at the gym promises themselves an hour a day, every day, forever. By February, the plan is gone. Not from laziness: the plan never fit their actual life.
Prayer and meditation can go the same way. It's easy to picture the ideal version, the saint up at three, sitting still for hours, and to count anything less as failure.
This is the last day of this stretch on simran, and it isn't a new technique. It's a plan that fits you.

teach.h: A WEEK OF TOOLS, NOT RULES.
teach.b: Look back at the week's tools. Waheguru on the breath, Wahe in, Guru out. Satnam: true name.
Coming back when the mind runs off. The early hour, amrit vela. The mala, bead by bead.
And the Name running under your work. None of these are rules you must follow. They're tools, and Sikhs use them in many combinations.
Some do simran for an hour before dawn. Some do five minutes on the bus. Some join the sangat for simran at the gurdwara, the whole room repeating Waheguru in rhythm.
The Sikh code of conduct asks Sikhs to rise early and meditate on the Name, and many take that as a daily anchor, but the Gurus never set a minimum number of minutes.
What the Guru Granth Sahib keeps returning to is remembering, done again and again, not once in a heroic burst. So, three questions.
When? A time that already exists in your day: waking up, a coffee, a commute, before sleep. Where?
A real place: the edge of the bed, a chair, the car before you go in. How long? Smaller than you think.
Five minutes, done every day, beats an hour done once. And if a day gets missed, simran already has its answer. You just come back.

how: Sikhs keep simran in many ways: alone before dawn, in short moments through the day, or together in the gurdwara where the sangat repeats Waheguru in rhythm.

o: a private mantra given to you by a teacher
a steady habit of remembering, sized to your life
a set number of prayers every Sikh must say

games.q: this week's tools — tap the pairs.

s: the Gurus set a minimum number of minutes for simran
they praise steadiness, but set no minimum length.

games.q: you want to start simran. which plan is most likely to last?
o: an hour every day at 3 a.m., starting tomorrow.
five minutes at a time that's already in your day.
games.why: steadiness is what the hymns praise. five minutes, kept daily, is a real practice; the heroic plan rarely survives February.

practice: Walk through tomorrow in your mind, from waking up, and find a gap: before you check your phone, right after you drop the kids, when you park the car.
Picture yourself there doing five minutes of whichever simran you liked best this week, or, if you're here to learn, five minutes of quiet breathing. Stay in that picture a while.

wordCard.voice: Your simran. Remembering the Name, at a time, a place and a length that fit your real life, done steadily.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: simran, remembering, from a root meaning to remember.

carryVoice: Your line: your five minutes. Small, steady, and yours to come back to. That's day one hundred twenty-seven.
